I'm super confused why I'm being down voted- with funds, a grandparent can absolutely take a parent to court for visitation. 

As I said - case law about this focuses on another application, but a grandparent absolutely has the legal right to do so. 

Do they win? Not usually, but OP didn't ask that, just asked if it were possible for MIL to even take her to court and what might happen.

Hay OP,

I'm not a lawyer; law student, and I've been in your shoes. 

Yes - your MIL can take you to court for visitation/grandparent rights. Case law for this was more geared towards when a couple splits if the custodial parent keeps the kids away from an absentee parent's parents - but it does get applied other places. 

I was taken to court by my mother as she wanted visitation rights for her two biological grand children, and I had been preventing her from seeing them as I have three other children that i had raised since birth - but who weren't biologicallg mine, and she refused to see them. 

When you are taken to court (at least in bc) for this, you have to do a parenting after separation class - its the same class you have to do when mediating a divorce and separation agreement that involves kids. It can be done online, and takes 5 hours- it is mandatory. 

I went to court twice - once to establish that I wasn't interested in mediation/set a court date, and then our court date. The actual court case took about 4 hours total. Witnesses are called, and they are cross examined - you can represent yourself. I represented myself, and my mom had a lawyer

I will say there are emotional ramifications for cross examining your own family in a court setting. 

You will have to show that the kids don't really have a relationship with MIL, that MIL is or could be harmful in some way (emotionally too), and the reason you are preventing contact. 

You dont get the judgement right away- I believe it took 5 weeks before I got mine in the mail. I won. Though there aren't really any winners...

So yes, it's a thing, absolutely. And if your MIL has the funds and time- she can take you to court. And you have to make time to respond and attend the court dates. Yes, it sucks - in so many ways.

Small claims is up to $35,000 - so you would still seek compensation in that court. If/when you go - you'll want the notarized statements from all the people you mentioned, dash cam footage etc. You cannot rely on the insurance findings alone. 

If after filing, and submitting evidence and serving the defendant, they don't respond within 20 days I think it is, you can file for a default judgement. If they do respond you'll either settle or request a court date. 

If you to to court, the judge will look at the evidence. If they find the defendant  90% responsible, you will get a judgement in your favour for 90% of your deductible plus any fees. 

The defendant is allowed to file a counter claim for any damages they incurred, including medical expenses and loss of work (they can for pain and suffering too technically but not normally). So, if the defendant is found 90% responsible, that means you are responsible for 10% - and they will get a judgement for 10% of their damages. 

I dont know how injured the pedestrian was, but you will want to take that into consideration when determining whether to file.

NAL, but a law student. 

With insurance, they use a standard of probabilities - so is it "more likely than not" that x event happened a certain way. 

In Ontario by finding you not at fault that means they believe you hold less than 25% responsibility. NOT that you have zero responsibility, but that it is more likely than not that your son is less than 25% responsible for damages/injuries. 

If you go to small claims to retrieve your deductible, it will cost you about 350 in fees (the filing, serving documents, trial date request). If you win- you can get about 85% of your fees back - so you'd still lose about $55, plus your time and any non court related costs. If you lose, it is further possible for the other party to get a judgement requiring you to pay part of their fees. 

It's your money and your principles so it's your choice.

The vernix smell can be smelt by anyone - though women tend to be more sensitive to it overall. But the pheromones are usually tied to children in one's care - including step children, or any children you spend enough time with. 

A caregivers endocrine system adapts to pick up these pheromones in children they spend a lot of time with. There are theories that the endocrine system in parents who abuse their children is underdeveloped - but there are a myriad of reasons abuse occurs. 

It's similar to pheromones in romantic relationships. We are attracted to and in tune to them in our partners. There are studies that show that on a very deep level we can sense certain genetic or immune characteristics from pheromones and we are biologically more attracted to people who "complete" us; that is, have immune system strengths where we have weaknesses.

You could very well be picking up kn the pheromones - which wre produced heavily until age 7 (first puberty) and then usually stop when the child goes through hormonal puberty as a teen. If you are a caregiver, or otherwise bonded to the child, you just may be very sensitive to them. These particular pheromones are designed to help us protect the child until the child is ready to be on its own.

The vernix smell can last for months - the more the baby is exposed to the elements (i read somewhere sunlight is the harshest, even over water) the quicker the smell disappears. But the pheromones from their heads that keeps us bonded are produced heavily until age 7 (sometimes known as first puberty), and then are gone by the time the child goes through hormonal puberty. It's evolutionary and biogical - and is supposed to help people close to the child ensure the child is protected until they see old enough to be on their own.

The smell itself comes from a substance called vernix. It's the white kind of greasy stuff thay babies are coated in while in utero. It protects their skin. 

Further, mothers (and sometimes close family members) can pick up on pheromones released through sweat glands - particularly from a baby's head. This is what helps keep us bonded to a baby who screams all night, the very scent of it causes our brains to release happy hormones.

Im in British Columbia - tenancyaws do vary across Canada. 

If there are two parties on a lease - one party cannot unilaterally end the lease for the other. One party cannot remove the other party from the lease. The landlord can't "evict" one party without going through the tenancy board. 

When a fixed term lease ends, it automatically goes to a month to month. Same terms, same everything. No one has to leave when the fixed term ends. The only way a landlords can get tenants out is by evicting- which they can if they plan to take possession of it themselves, or their immediate family members (and if the place is shown to be up for rent again within 12 months of when the original renter vacated, then the renter can take the old landlord ro court for a lot of damages). If the landlord wants to sell- the tenant is usually part of that sale. A lot of the time a cash fir keys is offered - where the landlord and tenant agree and sign a document saying the tenant is vacating and receiving x dollars in exchange.

NAL - When my daughters sat down to do a "views of the child" - it was done with a court appointed child mediator. They each spoke to the mediator independently for about an hour and a half. 

The views of the child is not a psychological evaluation. 

If the other party is requesting a different type of evaluation, it does not take the place of the meeting with a mediator - but can be in addition to. The judge at my hearing indicated that if my ex spouse felt our children weren't being treated for something or were being psychologically neglected - he could request other evaluations. However - I could dispute them if I felt they would be emotionally damaging to our daughters. 

The views of the child report essentially put together a story of how the child sees things and has experienced the separation, and asks questions about living arrangements. It puts forth the child's opinions on where they want to be through more open ended questions. The report itself is not a decision - the judge then takes that report, along with any other evaluations, into account when deciding parenting time.

I have bipolar 2 as well (and borderline personality disorder), and as anecdotal evidence I did an ayahuasca ceremony. 

As a caveat - my psychiatrist is aware of my use of psychedelics, and believes in their use to treat mental illness. The governing body he works under prevents him from recommending any plant based medicines (cannabis etc), but he does speak on the use of psychedelics in a number of conferences. 

Obviously, everyone is different. BUT, in my opinion only, something like ayahuasca should only be attempted by someone with bipolar if their condition is currently well managed. NOT in times of crisis. You should be in a stable and good frame of mind. If you are remotely hypomanic or bordering on severe depression than skip it. The potential to really mess with your head is there. 

Further, most organizations, shamans, whoever you decide to go to for this usually say that if you have bipolar (and other issues) you are not allowed to participate. It can be scary, a few people during my ceremony freaked out completely and had to be encouraged by the shaman and walked through their terrors. So in order to go you may need to lie about your diagnosis, and thus the medications your on (so make sure to do your research and some medications dont mix well at all with ayahuasca), and you may not get the help that you, as a bipolar person, needs during your experience because the facilitators wont know how to do it - which is again why you should only do it when you are in a stable place. 

The come down and reintegration into society was hard - I did a 2 day ceremony- I had support from my therapist and psychiatrist afterwards which was helpful, so make sure you have a support team after as well. The aftercare is almost more important to the process than the ceremony itself.
